newsitem.title: USA: Mother of Rabin's killer suspects wider plot.
newsitem.headline: Mother of Rabin's killer suspects wider plot.

text.p: The mother of the man who killed Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin said in an article published on Tuesday she believed her son did not act alone and the Israeli domestic secret service Shin Bet might have played a role in the assassination.
In an article in George magazine, Geula Amir wrote that she did not believe her son Yigal's statement that he acted alone.

"I believe he did that not to implicate others," she said, adding that her suspicions of a wider plot have been fuelled by her son's closeness to a rightwing militant later accused of being an informer and even an agent provocateur for Shin Bet.
She said she believes the alleged informer manipulated her son into plotting to harm Rabin and that Shin Bet was aware of his actions.

John Kennedy Jr., publisher of the monthly political magazine, said Amir family representatives approached him about publishing the article, "hoping that my own family history would bring added attention to their story and they were probably right." He was referring to the mystery over whether his father, President John F. Kennedy, was killed by a lone assassin.
Kennedy also stressed that Mrs. Amir's article was the work of "an anguished mother and a staunch rightwinger" and was not intended to be an objective account.
A spokeswoman for the magazine said Mrs. Amir wrote the article in collaboration with her lawyers.

Mrs. Amir said she believed rightwing militant Avishai Raviv spent months talking her son into harming Rabin and that he did so as an agent provocateur for Shin Bet, which she claims wanted an act to discredit the Israeli rightwing opposed to Rabin's efforts at peace with Palestinians.

She said she believed those manipulating her son did not plan for Rabin to die and that when her son shot Rabin to death at a peace rally on Nov. 4, 1995, the shouts of "blanks, blanks" that filled the air came from Shin Bet agents and not her son as testimony had it at his trial.
"Shin Bet agents are trained to shout out 'blanks, blanks' during security drills," she said, adding her son was able to inflitrate the area where Rabin spoke with great ease.
Mrs. Amir added, "The Shin Bet could have arrested Yigal at any time in the weeks before the rally and charged him with plotting to kill Rabin.

"But the impact on the public would have been much more dramatic if Shin Bet agents heroically foiled an attempt on the prime minister's life. But something went terribly wrong. The bullets were not blanks and the gun not a toy."

She criticised the official Israeli investigation for not making public what it had discovered about Raviv: "The offical investigation of Raviv's relationship with Yigal remains shrouded in secrecy. Labour, of course, wanted no further probing into a potentially explosive scandal. Likud, having forced national elections ... preferred to put the issue to rest."

She added, "I believe Raviv enjoyed the full backing and protection of Shin Bet. He assaulted a member of the Knesset and did not spend a day in jail. ... Raviv's lawlessness had to have sent the message to potential extremists that violence could be employed with impunity."
Mrs. Amir applied for a United States visa in January to make a lecture tour in connection with the article but a State Department spokesman said no decision had yet been made.
